name: CONCAT

args.name: text1
args.about: text, a cell or a range of cells to join

about: Joins pieces of text into one, with nothing between them.

example.why: Ada, a space and Lovelace are joined end to end.

notes: TEXTJOIN puts a separator between the pieces and can skip empty cells.

name: TEXTSPLIT

args.name: ignore_empty
args.about: TRUE to skip empty pieces (FALSE if left out)

args.name: match_mode
args.about: 1 to ignore upper and lower case (0 if left out)

args.name: pad_with
args.about: what fills gaps in short rows (#N/A if left out)

about: Cuts text into pieces at a separator and spreads them across cells.

example.why: The text is cut at each comma; red shows here and green and blue spill into the next two cells.

name: CONCATENATE

args.name: text1
args.about: text or a cell to join

about: Joins pieces of text into one, with nothing between them.

example.why: Lovelace, a comma and space, and Ada are joined end to end.

notes: An older name: use CONCAT, which also takes ranges, or TEXTJOIN.

name: EXACT
about: Tells whether two pieces of text are exactly the same, upper and lower case included.

example.why: The letters match but abc is lower case and ABC is upper case.

notes: To compare without caring about case, use =A2=B2.

name: FIND

args.name: start_num
args.about: which character to start from (1 if left out)

about: Gives the position where one piece of text first appears inside another, minding upper and lower case.

example.why: The @ is the fourth character of ada@example.com.

notes: Gives #VALUE! when the text isn't found. SEARCH ignores case and allows wildcards.

name: LEFT

args.name: num_chars
args.about: how many characters (1 if left out)

about: Gives the first few characters of a piece of text.

example.why: The first two characters of UK-1042.

name: LEN
about: Counts the characters in a piece of text, spaces included.

example.why: Desk lamp has eight letters and a space.

name: LOWER
about: Turns all the letters in a piece of text into lower case.

example.why: Every capital letter becomes small.

name: MID

args.name: start_num
args.about: the position of the first character to take

about: Gives some characters from the middle of a piece of text.

example.why: Four characters starting at the fourth: 1042.

name: REPT
about: Repeats a piece of text a number of times.

example.why: The star is written 3 times.

name: RIGHT

args.name: num_chars
args.about: how many characters (1 if left out)

about: Gives the last few characters of a piece of text.

example.why: The last four characters of UK-1042.

name: SEARCH

args.name: find_text
args.about: the text to look for; ? stands for any one character and * for any run

args.name: start_num
args.about: which character to start from (1 if left out)

about: Gives the position where one piece of text first appears inside another, ignoring upper and lower case.

example.why: Apple starts at the ninth character; the capital A doesn't matter.

notes: Gives #VALUE! when the text isn't found. FIND minds case.

name: SUBSTITUTE

args.name: instance_num
args.about: which one to replace (all if left out)

about: Replaces some text with other text wherever it appears.

example.why: Every dash becomes a space.

notes: REPLACE changes text at a given position instead.

name: REGEXEXTRACT

args.name: pattern
args.about: the regular expression to look for

args.name: return_mode
args.about: 0 for the first match, 1 for all matches, 2 for the parts of the first match (0 if left out)

args.name: case_sensitivity
args.about: 1 to ignore upper and lower case (0 if left out)

about: Gives the part of a piece of text that matches a regular expression.

example.why: [0-9]+ matches a run of digits: 4521.

name: REGEXREPLACE

args.name: pattern
args.about: the regular expression to look for

args.name: occurrence
args.about: which match to replace (all if left out)

args.name: case_sensitivity
args.about: 1 to ignore upper and lower case (0 if left out)

about: Replaces the parts of a piece of text that match a regular expression.

example.why: Every space matches and is replaced by nothing.

name: REGEXTEST

args.name: pattern
args.about: the regular expression to look for

args.name: case_sensitivity
args.about: 1 to ignore upper and lower case (0 if left out)

about: Tells whether a piece of text matches a regular expression.

example.why: SW1A starts with two capitals then a digit.

name: T
about: Gives the value if it is text, and empty text otherwise.

example.why: Lamp is text, so it comes back as it is; =T(B2) would give empty text.

name: TEXT

args.name: value
args.about: the number or date to show

about: Shows a number as text in a format you choose.

example.why: The number gets a thousands comma and two decimal places.

name: TEXTAFTER

args.name: instance_num
args.about: which one to take the text after; negative counts from the end (1 if left out)

args.name: match_mode
args.about: 1 to ignore upper and lower case (0 if left out)

args.name: match_end
args.about: 1 to treat the end of the text as a delimiter (0 if left out)

args.name: if_not_found
args.about: what to give when the delimiter isn't there (#N/A if left out)

about: Gives the text that comes after a delimiter.

example.why: Everything after the @.

name: TEXTBEFORE

args.name: instance_num
args.about: which one to take the text before; negative counts from the end (1 if left out)

args.name: match_mode
args.about: 1 to ignore upper and lower case (0 if left out)

args.name: match_end
args.about: 1 to treat the end of the text as a delimiter (0 if left out)

args.name: if_not_found
args.about: what to give when the delimiter isn't there (#N/A if left out)

about: Gives the text that comes before a delimiter.

example.why: Everything before the @.

name: TEXTJOIN

args.name: delimiter
args.about: what to put between the pieces, like ", "

args.name: text1
args.about: text, a cell or a range to join

about: Joins pieces of text into one, with a separator between them.

example.why: The empty cell is skipped and the rest are joined with a comma and space.

name: TRIM
about: Takes away spaces at the start and end, and leaves single spaces between words.

example.why: The outer spaces go and the run of three between the words becomes one.

name: UNICODE

args.name: text
args.about: the text whose first character to look at

about: Gives the Unicode number of the first character of a piece of text.

example.why: The euro sign is Unicode character 8364.

notes: UNICHAR does the opposite.

name: UNICHAR
about: Gives the character with a Unicode number.

example.why: Unicode character 8364 is the euro sign.

notes: UNICODE does the opposite.

name: CHAR
about: Gives the character with a code number from 1 to 255.

example.why: Character 65 is a capital A.

notes: For characters beyond 255 use UNICHAR. CODE does the opposite.

name: CLEAN
about: Takes away characters that can't be printed, like line breaks.

example.why: CHAR(10) is a line break, which can't be printed, so it is taken away.

notes: TRIM takes away extra spaces.

name: CODE

args.name: text
args.about: the text whose first character to look at

about: Gives the code number of the first character of a piece of text.

example.why: The first character, A, has code 65.

notes: CHAR does the opposite. For characters beyond 255 use UNICODE.

name: ASC
about: Changes full-width (double-byte) letters and digits into normal half-width ones.

example.why: The wide characters typed in a Japanese, Chinese or Korean layout become ordinary ones.

notes: Ordinary text is left as it is.

name: ARRAYTOTEXT

args.name: array
args.about: the cells to turn into text

args.name: format
args.about: 0 for a short list, 1 for the form you'd type in a formula (0 if left out)

about: Turns a range of cells into one piece of text.

example.why: The values are joined with a comma and a space.

name: DOLLAR

args.name: decimals
args.about: how many decimal places (2 if left out)

about: Shows a number as money text, with a currency sign and thousands commas.

example.why: The number is rounded to two places and gets a dollar sign and a comma.

name: ENCODEURL

args.name: text
args.about: the text to put in a web address

about: Makes text safe to use in a web address, by writing spaces and symbols as % codes.

example.why: Each space becomes %20 and the & becomes %26.

name: ECMA.CEILING

args.name: significance
args.about: the multiple to round up to

about: Rounds a number up to the nearest multiple of another number.

example.why: The next multiple of 0.5 above 4.32 is 4.5.

notes: CEILING.MATH and CEILING do the same.

name: FINDB

args.name: start_num
args.about: which character to start from (1 if left out)

about: The same as FIND: in Calc it counts characters, not bytes.

example.why: With ordinary letters every character is one byte, so the @ is at 4 as with FIND.

notes: In some other spreadsheet apps, with Chinese, Japanese or Korean set as the editing language, FINDB counts each double-byte character as two. Calc always counts every character as one, so FINDB gives the same as FIND. Use FIND.

name: FIXED

args.name: decimals
args.about: how many decimal places (2 if left out)

args.name: no_commas
args.about: TRUE to leave out the thousands commas (FALSE if left out)

about: Shows a number as text, rounded to some decimal places, with thousands commas.

example.why: Rounded to one place, with a comma for the thousands.

name: LEFTB

args.name: num_bytes
args.about: how many characters (1 if left out)

about: The same as LEFT: in Calc it counts characters, not bytes.

example.why: With ordinary letters every character is one byte, so this gives the first two characters.

notes: In some other spreadsheet apps, with Chinese, Japanese or Korean set as the editing language, LEFTB counts each double-byte character as two. Calc always counts every character as one, so LEFTB gives the same as LEFT. Use LEFT.

name: LENB
about: The same as LEN: in Calc it counts characters, not bytes.

example.why: Ordinary letters and spaces are one byte each.

notes: In some other spreadsheet apps, with Chinese, Japanese or Korean set as the editing language, LENB counts each double-byte character as two. Calc always counts every character as one, so LENB gives the same as LEN. Use LEN.

name: MIDB
about: The same as MID: in Calc it counts characters, not bytes.

example.why: With ordinary letters every character is one byte, so this is the same as MID.

notes: In some other spreadsheet apps, with Chinese, Japanese or Korean set as the editing language, MIDB counts each double-byte character as two. Calc always counts every character as one, so MIDB gives the same as MID. Use MID.

name: NUMBERVALUE

args.name: text
args.about: the text to turn into a number

args.name: decimal_separator
args.about: the character used for the decimal point

about: Turns text into a number, with the decimal and thousands separators you say.

example.why: The comma is the decimal point and the dot separates thousands.

name: PROPER
about: Gives each word a capital first letter and makes the rest small.

example.why: Each word starts with a capital and the other letters become small.

name: REPLACE

args.name: start_num
args.about: the position of the first character to replace

about: Replaces some characters at a given position with other text.

example.why: The first two characters, UK, become FR.

notes: SUBSTITUTE replaces by matching text instead of by position.

name: REPLACEB
about: The same as REPLACE: in Calc it counts characters, not bytes.

example.why: With ordinary letters every character is one byte, so this is the same as REPLACE.

notes: In some other spreadsheet apps, with Chinese, Japanese or Korean set as the editing language, REPLACEB counts each double-byte character as two. Calc always counts every character as one, so REPLACEB gives the same as REPLACE. Use REPLACE.

name: RIGHTB

args.name: num_bytes
args.about: how many characters (1 if left out)

about: The same as RIGHT: in Calc it counts characters, not bytes.

example.why: With ordinary letters every character is one byte, so this is the same as RIGHT.

notes: In some other spreadsheet apps, with Chinese, Japanese or Korean set as the editing language, RIGHTB counts each double-byte character as two. Calc always counts every character as one, so RIGHTB gives the same as RIGHT. Use RIGHT.

name: SEARCHB

args.name: find_text
args.about: the text to look for; ? and * work as wildcards

args.name: start_num
args.about: which character to start from (1 if left out)

about: The same as SEARCH: in Calc it counts characters, not bytes.

example.why: With ordinary letters every character is one byte, so Apple is found at 9 as with SEARCH.

notes: In some other spreadsheet apps, with Chinese, Japanese or Korean set as the editing language, SEARCHB counts each double-byte character as two. Calc always counts every character as one, so SEARCHB gives the same as SEARCH. Use SEARCH.

name: UPPER
about: Turns all the letters in a piece of text into capitals.

example.why: Every small letter becomes a capital.

name: VALUE

args.name: text
args.about: text that looks like a number

about: Turns text that looks like a number into a number.

example.why: The text 42.5 becomes the number 42.5, which can then be doubled.

notes: NUMBERVALUE lets you say which decimal separator the text uses.

name: VALUETOTEXT

args.name: value
args.about: the value to turn into text

args.name: format
args.about: 0 for plain, 1 to put text in quotes (0 if left out)

about: Turns any value into text.

example.why: The number 120 becomes the text 120, then words are joined on.
